d: From a fresh VPS to a Laravel app on HTTPS in five commands.
x: This page takes you from a fresh Ubuntu VPS to a Laravel app on HTTPS. Each step shows the commands and what they print; click a terminal to skip to the end of it. You need a VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 and a public IP, a domain whose DNS you can change, and a Git repository. 1. Install Cipi on the server SSH into the fresh server as root (or a sudo user) and run the installer. It asks for your SSH public key first, shows its plan, and sets up the stack in about ten minutes. Details, requirements and the non-interactive variant are in Install Cipi . $ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | ba

SSH into the fresh server as root (or a sudo user) and run the installer. It asks for your SSH public key first, shows its plan, and sets up the stack in about ten minutes. Details, requirements and the non-interactive variant are in Install Cipi . $ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash

h: 2. Log in as the cipi user
x: Root login over SSH is disabled after the install. Connect as cipi with your key and prefix commands with sudo , which works without a password for cipi only. $ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10 $ sudo cipi status

The interactive wizard starts with numbered menus, the default pre-selected: the app type ( Laravel , custom, or a Node spa / static / ssr app), then for Laravel PHP-FPM or Octane (FrankenPHP) and the database engine (MariaDB or PostgreSQL). It then asks for a username, primary domain, Git repository URL (SSH format) and branch when applicable, PHP version, and an optional asset build such as npm ci && npm run build that runs inside every deploy. Laravel apps always require a repository; for custom apps you can leave the repository empty to host the site via SFTP only — see custom apps . Before the summary Cipi tests the deploy key against the repository and, when it cannot read it, offers to save the forge token and registers the key for you. $ sudo cipi app create cipi app create cipi app create --octane # Laravel Octane (FrankenPHP) Or pass all flags directly to skip interactive mode: cipi app create \ --user=myapp \ --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git \ --branch=main \ --php=8.5 At the end, Cipi prints a credentials summary — save it, shown only once — including the server's public IP address (for DNS configuration), the SSH deploy key, database credentials, a ready-to-use mariadb+ssh:// connection URL for GUI clients (TablePlus, DBeaver, Sequel Pro), webhook URL, and webhook token.

h: 4. Add the deploy key to your Git provider
x: If you have configured a token for your Git provider via cipi git — GitHub, GitLab, Cursor Origin, AWS CodeCommit, Bitbucket Cloud or Azure DevOps since v5.2.3 — this step is automatic — Cipi adds the deploy key and creates the webhook for you. See Git auto-setup for details. Otherwise, copy the ssh-ed25519 ... key shown after app creation and add it as a Deploy Key in your repository, then confirm with cipi git check myapp : GitHub: Repository → Settings → Deploy keys → Add deploy key GitLab: Repository → Settings → Repository → Deploy keys Bitbucket Cloud: Repository settings → Access keys Azure DevOps: User settings → SSH public keys

Cipi uses the database driver for cache, sessions, and queues. A Laravel 11+ skeleton already ships those migrations; on an older project run these once, commit, and push the generated migrations: php artisan cache:table php artisan session:table php artisan queue:table php artisan migrate Cipi automatically runs artisan migrate --force on every deploy. The cache, session, and queue tables will be created on first deploy if you commit the migrations. Why not Valkey (Redis) by default? Cipi installs Valkey on every server, but it is one instance with one password for all the apps of the server: an app that has it can read, and flush, the cache, sessions and queues of every other app. The database driver keeps each app inside its own database and user. Valkey is a deliberate choice per app — faster queues and cache, Horizon, Reverb scaling — and how to switch, with a distinct REDIS_PREFIX per app, is in Valkey . The phpredis extension is already installed.

cipi deploy myapp Deployer clones your repo into a new releases/N/ directory, runs composer install --no-dev , links .env and storage/ , runs migrations, runs artisan optimize , creates storage:link , swaps the current symlink atomically, and restarts queue workers. Zero downtime. $ sudo cipi deploy myapp

cipi ssl install myapp Certbot obtains a Let's Encrypt certificate for the domain and its aliases, Cipi writes the HTTPS vhost (HTTP redirects to HTTPS) and updates APP_URL in .env . Your Laravel app is now live on https://myapp.com . The DNS of every name must already point to the server and port 80 must be open. $ sudo cipi ssl install myapp Behind the Cloudflare proxy , prefer cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare (works with the proxy on) and set SSL/TLS to Full (strict) — never Flexible. Subdomains for tenants ( *.myapp.com ): see Wildcard domains & SSL .

If you or your clients prefer a browser, install the REST API and the panel. Each needs its own domain pointed at the server. The panel can then manage this server and any other Cipi server you connect. See Install the panel . $ sudo cipi api api.example.com $ sudo cipi gui panel.example.com

Cipi sets up the firewall, fail2ban, swap and kernel parameters, which needs a kernel of its own. Since v5.5.0 the installer checks the environment before anything else. In a container it stops and names what it found — OpenVZ / Virtuozzo, LXC, Docker, Podman, WSL, OrbStack, systemd-nspawn, or the raw type — says why Cipi cannot run there, and what to use instead. (Before, a container image without bc failed the Ubuntu version check with a confusing requires Ubuntu 24.04+ (found: 24.04) ; the version check no longer needs bc , so a minimal image of a supported release on a real VM passes.) Full VMs and bare metal are not affected. Cipi does not run locally. It is not compatible with local dockerized environments. The installer may appear to succeed on a laptop VM or container, but SSL provisioning, domain routing, and production workflows will not work without a real public server. See Why not local? for the full explanation. C

Cipi installs a complete Laravel-ready production stack on Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 with a single command. The installer takes roughly 10 minutes and sets up Nginx, MariaDB, PHP, Valkey (optional PostgreSQL via cipi db install pgsql after install), Supervisor, Fail2ban, UFW, Certbot, Deployer, and the cipi CLI itself. $ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash

h: From zero to production in three steps
x: # 1 — on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 VPS, over SSH, as a user with sudo wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash # 2 — create the app (Laravel by default) cipi app create # 3 — deploy it and put it behind HTTPS cipi deploy myapp cipi ssl install myapp That is the whole path. First create an SSH key on your computer (below), then run the installer on the server — it will ask you to paste that public key. Everything after that is explained in the rest of this page. Run the installer on the server, not on your own machine. SSH into the fresh VPS first and run it there, as a user with sudo . Cipi provisions the whole box — it is not something you point at a remote host from your laptop.

h: Create an SSH key on your computer
x: Do this on your laptop or workstation , not on the VPS. The installer needs the public half of the key so it can lock down the server: after setup you SSH in as the cipi user with this key. Root SSH login is disabled. Never paste the private key. See if you already have one: ls ~/.ssh/*.pub If id_ed25519.pub or id_rsa.pub is listed, you already have a key — skip generation and copy the public file with the command below. If the folder is empty or the command errors, create a new Ed25519 key: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com" Press Enter to accept the default path ( ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ). Set a passphrase if you want (recommended). On macOS and Linux run this in Terminal; on Windows use PowerShell or WSL. Show the public key — this is the single line you will paste when the installer asks: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub It looks like ssh-ed25519 AAAA… comment . Copy the whole line: macOS: pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub Linux: xclip -sel clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (or copy from the terminal) Windows (PowerShell): Get-Content $env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub | Set-Clipboard Only the .pub file is public. The file named id_ed25519 (no extension) is the private key — keep it on your computer and never paste it into the installer or send it to the server.

h: Run the installer on the server
x: SSH into the fresh Ubuntu VPS as a user with sudo , then: wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash The wizard asks for the public key before any package is installed . Paste the line you copied above (accepted formats: ssh-ed25519 , ssh-rsa , ecdsa ); since 5.8.2 it then asks Add another SSH public key? [y/N] until you press Enter, so a second machine or a colleague's key goes in now, each shown with its fingerprint. Cipi sanitizes comments, carriage returns, and extra whitespace, then creates a dedicated cipi Linux user for admin SSH access and hardens SSH: root login disabled, cipi public-key only (group cipi-ssh ), app users (group cipi-apps ) can connect with password. Login attempts are limited to 3 with a 20-second grace period; X11 forwarding is disabled. With the keys in, the installer shows what it is about to set up — the server's IP, hostname and OS, the SSH access (your keys, root without SSH login, passwords off), the stack, and which passwords it will generate — and asks Proceed with the installation? [Y/n] . Answer n and nothing on the machine has changed. The installer also generates a random 40-character root password , stores it in /etc/cipi/server.json , and displays it in the installation summary. It is not an SSH password: root SSH login is disabled. It is what you type when, already logged in as the cipi user with your key, you run su root . Keep it in a password manager.

For automated setups, pass your SSH public key via the SSH_PUBKEY environment variable to skip the interactive prompt (several keys: one per line). Without a terminal the installer asks nothing else either: no plan confirmation, no “saved?” question, no optional wizard. SSH_PUBKEY="ssh-ed25519 AAAA..." wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash

ssh ubuntu@your-server-ip sudo -s wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash At the end of the installation you will see the credentials, one block each with the same rows — User: , Password: , where to reach it — for Root, MariaDB and Valkey (and PostgreSQL, Meilisearch and the backup key once they exist), the databases with a ready connection URL through SSH. Save them immediately : since 5.8.2 the installer waits until you answer y to Have you saved these credentials? before it prints anything else, and only then offers what is optional. Since 5.9.0 that starts with your Git provider: the installer asks where your repositories are (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps), says where to create an access token and which permissions it needs, and saves it — with a token, cipi app create adds the deploy key and the push webhook to each repository by itself; without one you add both by hand for every app. Enter skips it ( cipi git github-token <token> does the same later). Then two questions ( Install the panel API now? , Install the web GUI on this server now? ). Lost them later? sudo cipi credentials prints the same card again, and sudo cipi credentials export writes a CSV ( title,url,username,password,notes ) any password manager imports. Credentials are stored in /etc/cipi/server.json , which — like all Cipi configuration files — is encrypted at rest using AES-256-CBC via the built-in Vault system. Credentials, SSH keys, .env files, and database dumps are protected both on disk and during transfer (via Sync encrypted archives). Cipi also enforces GDPR-compliant log retent

After installation, admin access uses public-key authentication as the cipi user (root login is disabled). App users can SSH directly with ssh myapp@server-ip and the password generated at app creation. To run cipi commands, connect as cipi and either prefix them with sudo (allowed without a password, for cipi only) or become root with su root and the root password from the installation summary . Do not use sudo -s : the cipi user's own password is random and never shown, so sudo has nothing to accept for anything but cipi . # 1. connect to the server (key-based auth only) ssh cipi@your-server-ip # 2a. run a cipi command — no password needed cipi@server:~$ sudo cipi status # 2b. or become root (root password from the installation summary) cipi@server:~$ su root # 3. as root, every cipi command works without sudo root@server:~# cipi status root@server:~# cipi app list # 4. to work as an app user, switch with su root@server:~# su - myapp

Cipi brings a complete, production-ready stack to your Ubuntu server. Here is everything that gets installed and configured: Component Role Ubuntu Base OS (24.04 or 26.04 LTS) Nginx Web server, reverse proxy, SSL termination. Since v4.5.9 , mainline nginx from nginx.org (1.31.9+ since v5.9.1 , see nginx security ) with max_headers 1000 for HTTP/2 hardening — not the Ubuntu archive package PHP-FPM Default PHP runtime per app (8.6 installed on a new server since v5.9.1, 8.5 before; 8.3–8.6 available; packages.sury.org, ondrej/php, or Ubuntu main per release) Laravel Octane Optional FrankenPHP HTTP server per Laravel app (since v5.0 ) — cipi app create --octane ; FPM and Octane apps coexist on the same server MariaDB Default relational database (drop-in MySQL replacement, port 3306). Optional PostgreSQL via cipi db install pgsql (port 5432) since v4.8.0 Valkey In-memory store for cache, sessions, queues, broadcast (BSD-licensed Redis fork) Supervisor Process manager for Laravel queue workers, Octane, Horizon, and Reverb Deployer Zero-downtime deployment tool — 8.0.5, from its GitHub release, SHA-256 checked (since v5.10.0) Certbot Let's Encrypt SSL certificates UFW Firewall (ports 22, 80, 443) Fail2ban Progressive brute-force protection with recidive jail unattended-upgrades Automatic security patches Composer PHP dependency manager cipi CLI Server management and orchestration

Each app runs in a fully isolated environment. Laravel is the default — zero-downtime deploys, its own database, workers, scheduler and webhook — optionally served by Octane (FrankenPHP) instead of PHP-FPM. --custom is for simple sites (WordPress, static + PHP): a classic deploy into htdocs , a configurable docroot, no database, no .env , no cron, no workers. Area What Cipi gives you Web server Nginx with a per-app virtual host — PHP-FPM or Octane via proxy_pass , tuned for Laravel PHP & Composer Selectable per app, hot-swappable; settings managed with cipi ini across FPM and CLI Database MariaDB by default, optional PostgreSQL — a dedicated database and user per Laravel app Queue workers Supervisor pools per app — queue:work or Horizon; optional Reverb for WebSockets Deployments Deployer — atomic symlink, 5 releases, rollback, optional Node build; classic clone into htdocs for custom apps SSL Let's Encrypt via Certbot — HTTP-01 by default, optional DNS-01 (Cloudflare) with wildcards Security Fail2ban + UFW, a dedicated Linux user, its own FPM/Octane process and SSH key per app; opt-in CrowdSec and Cloudflare Zero Trust Healthchecks HTTP probes every 5 minutes, plus a post-deploy check with optional automatic rollback of a broken release; since 5.3, cipi monitor watches disk, services, workers, 5xx spikes and load Backups Backup profiles — what, how often, where, how long — S3 / S3-compatible / local, with client-side encryption Configuration Optional per-project cipi.yml for aliases, databases, workers, healthcheck, backups and the deploy branch — one file per environment

When you run cipi app create , Cipi creates a fully isolated environment for the app. Here is everything that gets set up: /home/myapp/ ← isolated Linux user (chmod 750) ├── .ssh/ │ ├── id_ed25519 ← deploy key (private) │ └── id_ed25519.pub ← deploy key (public — add to Git) ├── .deployer/ │ └── deploy.php ← Deployer config (auto-generated) ├── current -> releases/3/ ← symlink to active release ├── releases/ │ ├── 1/ │ ├── 2/ │ └── 3/ ← latest release (last 5 kept) ├── shared/ │ ├── .env ← auto-compiled by Cipi │ └── storage/ ← persistent storage └── logs/ ├── nginx-access.log ├── nginx-error.log ├── php-fpm-error.log ├── worker-default.log └── deploy.log In addition to the home directory, Cipi creates these system files: PHP-FPM pool: /etc/php/8.5/fpm/pool.d/ myapp .conf (user=myapp; omitted for Octane apps) Octane (v5+): Supervisor myapp -octane + Nginx proxy_pass → 127.0.0.1:81xx Nginx vhost: /etc/nginx/sites-available/ myapp Supervisor: /etc/supervisor/conf.d/ myapp .conf Crontab: * * * * * php artisan schedule:run MariaDB: database ' myapp ', user ' myapp '@'localhost' The .env is auto-compiled with all credentials — database name, password, webhook token, and APP_KEY . You never have to touch it manually, but you can always edit it with cipi app env myapp . If someone unpacks a zip as root or chmods .ssh to 775, cipi app fix-permissions (since v5.2.1 ) restores this layout. A blunt chown -R app:app is wrong: nginx writes vhost logs as www-data into logs/ ( 2775 setgid), the home must stay 750 so www-data (in the app group) can read the docroot, and .ssh must be 700 or

d: The cipi app create wizard and its flags for Laravel, Node and custom apps.
x: cipi app create supports three app types: Laravel (default), Node ( --node=spa|static|ssr , since v5.4.0 ) and Custom ( --custom ). Laravel apps get a fully isolated environment: Linux user, PHP-FPM pool or Laravel Octane (FrankenPHP) since v5.0 , Nginx vhost, database (MariaDB by default; optional PostgreSQL since v4.8.0 ), Supervisor worker, crontab entry, Deployer zero-downtime releases, SSH deploy key, and auto-compiled .env . Node apps build a React, Vue, Svelte, Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Astro or Remix project on every deploy — see Node apps . Custom apps are simpler — see custom apps fo

cipi app create Since v5.6.0 the wizard opens with numbered menus, the default pre-selected (press Enter to take it): the app type — Laravel, custom, or a Node spa / static / ssr app — then, for Laravel, PHP-FPM or Octane and the database engine (MariaDB or PostgreSQL, when both are installed). The details follow: username, domain, repository, branch, PHP version and an optional asset build such as npm ci && npm run build , which runs inside every deploy before the release goes live (the same setting as cipi app edit --node-build ; non-interactive: --node-build= ). A Node app asks for its framework (or build/output for a static site). Any type flag ( --custom , --octane , --node= , --framework= ) skips the menus, and without a terminal every default applies. Before the summary, the deploy key is tested against the repository ( git ls-remote as the app user, branch included). When it cannot read it, the summary says so and, on a terminal, Cipi offers to save or replace the forge token, registers the key and checks again — see Git auto-setup . cipi git check <app> repeats the test later.

cipi app create --octane cipi app create --octane=frankenphp # explicit (same as --octane) See Laravel Octane for requirements, convert, and how the vhost differs from FPM. Since v5.10.0 the new app is pinned to the newest FrankenPHP build already on the server, so create downloads nothing; on a server with no build yet the first deploy adopts the one Octane fetches.

cipi app create \ --user=myapp \ --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git \ --branch=main \ --php=8.5 # Laravel Octane (FrankenPHP) — v5.0+ cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --octane # optional PostgreSQL (v4.8.0+, after cipi db install pgsql) cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --engine=pgsql # since v5.9.0 a Laravel app gets a Valkey instance of its own (REDIS_* in its .env); # --valkey=shared keeps the server's shared instance for this app cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --valkey=shared # a staging app of the same repository (v5.8.0+): it reads cipi-staging.yml before cipi.yml cipi app create --user=myapp-stg --domain=staging.myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --branch=develop --env=staging --user Linux username for the app. Must be unique, lowercase, alphanumeric. --domain Primary domain (e.g. myapp.com ). Used for Nginx vhost and APP_URL . --repository SSH Git URL (e.g. git@github.com:you/repo.git ). Must be SSH, not HTTPS. --branch Branch to deploy. Defaults to main . --env Environment label for the app (since v5.8.0 ): lowercase letters, digits, - and _ , at most 32 characters, e.g. production or staging . Defaults to production , which is also what every app created before 5.8.0 is. Cipi writes it to the app's .env as APP_ENV (Laravel apps) and CIPI_ENV (Laravel and Node apps), cipi app show prints it, and it picks the cipi-<env>.yml the app reads before

d: Run apps on FrankenPHP, convert existing apps and pin builds.
x: Since v5.0 , Laravel apps can serve HTTP via Laravel Octane with the FrankenPHP server instead of a per-app PHP-FPM pool. Octane and classic FPM apps run side by side on the same Cipi server. What Cipi configures Allocates a localhost port in 8100–8999 and stores octane / octane_port in apps.json Nginx vhost uses proxy_pass to Octane and serves static files from current/public — no per-app FPM pool Supervisor program ${app}-octane alongside queue workers Deployer template laravel-octane.php links the app's pinned FrankenPHP build into each release and restarts / reloads Octane on deploy (v5.10

Allocates a localhost port in 8100–8999 and stores octane / octane_port in apps.json Nginx vhost uses proxy_pass to Octane and serves static files from current/public — no per-app FPM pool Supervisor program ${app}-octane alongside queue workers Deployer template laravel-octane.php links the app's pinned FrankenPHP build into each release and restarts / reloads Octane on deploy (v5.10.0+, see below) .env : OCTANE_SERVER=frankenphp , OCTANE_HTTPS=true

Your Laravel repository must include laravel/octane and run php artisan octane:install --server=frankenphp . Octane starts after the first successful deploy. Since v5.10.0 octane:install is still needed for the worker file and the .gitignore entries, but the frankenphp binary itself no longer comes from the repository or from Octane's own download: right after Composer vendors, the deploy links the app's pinned build into the release. If laravel/octane requires a newer FrankenPHP than the pin, the deploy stops before the release goes live and tells you to run cipi frankenphp upgrade <app> . # create an Octane app cipi app create --user=myapp --domain=myapp.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/myapp.git --octane # convert an existing FPM app → Octane (or the reverse) cipi app convert myapp --to=octane cipi app convert myapp --to=fpm # tune Octane workers (also see app limits) cipi app limits myapp --octane-workers=4 cipi app convert --to=octane|fpm rewrites the pool / vhost / Supervisor / Deployer template / .env , and re-applies SSL when a certificate is already present. Since v5.10.0 convert also turns the app's JIT off (the setting lives in a different place for FPM and Octane, so it is not carried over: run cipi app jit again after converting) and pins the app to a FrankenPHP build when it becomes Octane, or drops the pin when it goes back to FPM.

An Octane app answers on the PHP built into its FrankenPHP binary, which apt never patches. Up to 5.9.x that binary was nobody's: Laravel Octane downloads the latest FrankenPHP release into the project whenever it finds none there, octane:install puts frankenphp in .gitignore , and every release starts from a fresh checkout — so each deploy fetched whatever GitHub had that minute, a new PHP minor included. Since v5.10.0 the binary is Cipi's. Builds live in /opt/cipi-frankenphp/builds/ (root's, read-only to the apps), each with the FrankenPHP and PHP versions inside it; one is pinned per app, and every deploy links it into the new release before it goes live. Octane downloads nothing, and the PHP an app answers on changes only when you say so. cipi frankenphp # each app's build, the PHP inside, patched or not cipi frankenphp upgrade myapp # newest build on myapp's PHP minor cipi frankenphp upgrade --all cipi frankenphp use myapp <build> # pin a given build cipi frankenphp import ./frankenphp # a build made elsewhere — another PHP minor cipi frankenphp adopt myapp # pin the binary Octane downloaded cipi frankenphp remove <build> # or: prune Upgrades stay on the app's PHP minor and FrankenPHP major. Octane restarts, has to answer on its port, and the previous build comes back when it does not. A release on another PHP minor (or a new FrankenPHP major) is announced once, never applied: move the app with cipi app edit myapp --php=8.6 , then cipi frankenphp upgrade myapp . Several PHP minors side by side. An app on 8.5 and one on 8.6 run different builds on the same server. GitHu

d: Turn the OPcache JIT on or off for a single app.
x: Turn PHP's JIT compiler on for one app, PHP-FPM or Octane, without touching the others: cipi app jit myapp on # tracing, 128M buffer cipi app jit myapp on --mode=function --buffer=256M cipi app jit myapp off cipi app jit myapp [--json] # state, the PHP that answers, supported or not Checked before: the PHP that will run the app is asked to start with JIT in that mode — its CLI for PHP-FPM, the FrankenPHP binary for Octane. An extension that replaces the executor (Xdebug, pcov) or a build without JIT is refused there, before anything is written. Checked after: PHP-FPM has to be active, or Octan

d: SPA, static and SSR frontends built on every deploy.
x: Available since v5.4.0 . Until then a React or Vue SPA could only be a custom app serving a build committed to git: no build step, and client-side routes returned 404 on reload. SSR frameworks could not run at all. Node apps are an app type of their own, with the same lifecycle as Laravel apps — releases, rollback, webhook, SSL, basic auth, redirects and proxies , and the deploy audit ledger . # Vite + React/Vue/Svelte: build, then nginx serves dist/ with an /index.html fallback cipi app create --user=web --domain=web.example.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/web.git --node=spa --framework

Mode What nginx does spa Serves current/<output> ; unknown paths fall back to /index.html , so client-side routes survive a reload. assets/ , _astro/ , _nuxt/ , _app/immutable/ and static/ are cached as immutable ; *.html is no-cache . static The same without the fallback: $uri.html , then a real 404 with /404.html . ssr Proxies to a Node process on localhost through an upstream ( /etc/nginx/conf.d/cipi-node-<app>.conf ), with WebSocket upgrade and X-Forwarded-* headers.

--node=spa|static|ssr The app type and mode. --framework= next , nuxt , sveltekit , astro , remix (all ssr ) or vite ( spa , output dist ). A preset fills in the mode, build and start command; explicit flags win. --node-version=22|24 Node major (even, LTS majors only). Defaults to the server default . --build= Build command, default npm run build . --start= SSR start command — e.g. node build (SvelteKit), node .output/server/index.mjs (Nuxt). Next.js starts with next start -H 127.0.0.1 . Only a Node runner ( node npm npx pnpm yarn bun ) plus plain arguments is accepted. --output= Build directory for spa / static ; the deploy fails if <output>/index.html is missing. --health-path= SSR only: the path a new release must answer below 500 before it takes traffic (default / ).

The Deployer recipe installs dependencies from the lockfile — npm ci , pnpm install --frozen-lockfile , yarn install --immutable (or --frozen-lockfile ), bun install --frozen-lockfile ; npm install with a warning when there is no lockfile — then builds with NODE_ENV=production and telemetry off. shared/.env is a shared file, so frameworks read it at build time and SSR servers at runtime. Edit it with cipi app env .

An SSR app has two Supervisor programs, <app>-node-blue and <app>-node-green , each on its own localhost port in 3100–3999 , in /etc/supervisor/conf.d/<app>-node.conf (so cipi-worker restart cannot bounce both). Before deploy:symlink , the recipe calls cipi-node-switch : the new release starts on the idle slot; it must answer below 500 on the health path within 60 seconds; the upstream moves ( nginx -t , reload) and the old slot stops after a short drain. A process that exits or never answers is stopped, the old slot keeps serving, and the deploy fails before current moves. cipi deploy <app> --rollback switches back the same way, and cipi node restart <app> is blue/green too — no downtime. What the app user cannot change. cipi-node-switch runs as root through one sudoers rule per app. Only the release path comes from the caller, and it must be a release of that app; ports, start command, Node version and health path come from /var/lib/cipi/node/<app>.json , which only root writes. cipi-node-run reads .env as KEY=VALUE data and never sources it: PORT and HOST cannot be overridden, HOST , HOSTNAME and NITRO_HOST are forced to 127.0.0.1 , and the start command runs as argv with no shell.

A Node app has no Laravel to install Cipi Agent into, so /cipi/webhook goes to a receiver Cipi ships ( /usr/local/share/cipi/webhook.php ) through an on-demand PHP-FPM pool running as the app user: open_basedir limited to the home and the receiver, exec -family functions disabled, 2 MB body, POST only, never behind basic auth. It verifies GitHub and Bitbucket HMAC-SHA256 and GitLab / Azure DevOps tokens, deploys only pushes to the app's branch, and records the pusher, delivery id and commit in the audit ledger under claimed . With a Git provider token the webhook is registered for you, and cipi git refresh covers Node apps.

cipi node status shop # mode, commands, blue/green slots cipi node restart shop # zero-downtime restart (SSR) cipi node logs shop --lines=100 # log of the serving slot cipi app edit shop --start= "node .output/server/index.mjs" --health-path=/health cipi app edit web --node=static --output=dist cipi app edit shop --node-version=24 cipi app edit accepts --build= , --start= , --output= , --health-path= , --node-version= and --node=spa|static|ssr . cipi app show and cipi app list show the mode and slots; cipi app delete stops and removes both slots, the upstream and the state. The same settings can live in the repository as the node: section of cipi.yml , applied by the deploy itself. Runtimes are managed with cipi node . From the panel: API 1.31+ and the GUI create, edit and restart Node apps. Not yet: cipi sync skips Node apps with a message, and cipi app clone refuses them, as it does custom apps. No database is created with a Node app — add one with cipi db or the databases: section of cipi.yml .

d: WordPress, plain PHP and SFTP-only sites.
x: Creates a custom app with classic deploy (no zero-downtime): code is deployed into htdocs — no current / shared symlinks. Ideal for static sites, SPAs (Vue, React, Svelte), WordPress, other CMS, or any non-Laravel PHP project or framework. During creation you only choose the document root (default / , or e.g. www , dist , public ). Nginx is pre-configured with index index.html index.php , try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$args , and error_page 404 /404.html — no prompts for try_files or entry point. Git optional (SFTP-only) The Git repository is optional for custom apps. Laravel apps still requ

The Git repository is optional for custom apps. Laravel apps still require a repository. If you skip the repository for a custom app, Cipi creates /home/<app>/htdocs with a placeholder index.html and does not configure a deploy key or webhook — you upload files with SFTP (or SCP/rsync) to ~/htdocs as the app user. The onboarding output explains this “no repo — SFTP only” workflow. If you do provide a repository, behavior is unchanged: use cipi deploy <app> to pull code into htdocs .

h: What’s included and what you add
x: Custom apps have no database , no .env , no cron, and no queue workers. When a repository is configured, a deploy key and (with Git auto-setup) webhook are shown; for SFTP-only apps, those are omitted. The post-creation summary lists SSH access and next steps accordingly. If your custom app needs a database (e.g. WordPress, Drupal), create one with cipi db create --name=<app> after deployment. See cipi db for backup, restore, and password management. With Git — non-interactive example: cipi app create --custom --user=mysite --domain=mysite.com \ --repository=git@github.com:you/mysite.git --docroot=dist SFTP-only — omit --repository and --branch : cipi app create --custom --user=mysite --domain=mysite.com --docroot=dist With a repository, use cipi deploy <app> to deploy; code is cloned into /home/<app>/htdocs .

A custom app serves htdocs/ (or a subdirectory of it) as the Nginx document root, so a cipi.yml committed at the repository root used to answer at https://<domain>/cipi.yml . Since v5.2.3 every app vhost denies /cipi.yml and /cipi.yaml at any path — Laravel apps included, in case the file is ever copied into public/ . Since v5.8.0 the rule also covers the per-environment files, /cipi-<anything>.yml and .yaml ( cipi-staging.yml , cipi-production.yml , …); migration 5.8.0 updates the existing vhosts. Existing servers get the location block on update, without regenerating the vhost, so certbot's :443 block is left untouched. cipi yml also looks for the file in htdocs/ now, which is where a custom app's repository actually lives.

Available since v5.7.2 . cipi use <app> names the app the per-app commands act on when none is given: cipi deploy , cipi app logs|env|artisan|edit , cipi yml plan|apply , cipi worker list , cipi ssl install , cipi www … , cipi alias … , cipi health … and the others run against it and print → <app> (default app — cipi use) on stderr. The default is saved on the server ( /var/lib/cipi/default-app ); CIPI_APP=<app> does the same for one shell and wins over the file. cipi use shop # the default for the commands that need an app cipi deploy # → shop (default app — cipi use) cipi app logs --type=php cipi yml plan cipi use # show it cipi use --clear # remove it It fills in a missing app only where one is a required argument, so nothing that works changes meaning: a command for which a missing app means every app ( cipi git refresh|check , cipi scan ) keeps it, and cipi app delete|reset-password|reset-db-password|convert|clone and cipi db … still want the name. The panel API never gets a default. Tab-completion and cipi help use know the command.

Since v5.0 , clone an existing Laravel app into a new staging (or review) app with its own domain. Sets cloned_from in apps.json ; does not copy webhook or git IDs. If the source has Reverb, the clone gets its own port, credentials and public host (since v5.1.2 ) — it no longer inherits the production socket. See cipi app reverb . Since v5.2.2 , a cloned Scout app gets its own Meilisearch key and SCOUT_PREFIX ; the source's MEILISEARCH_* keys are excluded from the copied .env , because a clone that inherited them would reindex into production. See cipi search . Since v5.10.0 , an Octane clone is pinned to the same FrankenPHP build as its source when that build is a trusted one (fetched or imported; a build adopted from the source's own release is trusted only for the source, so the clone keeps the newest build it got at create). JIT is not copied: turn it on for the clone with cipi app jit if you want it there too. cipi app clone myapp --domain=staging.myapp.com cipi app clone myapp --domain=staging.myapp.com --name=myapp-stg --branch=develop --with-db cipi app clone myapp --domain=staging.myapp.com --branch=develop --env=staging # 5.8.0+: the clone reads cipi-staging.yml cipi app clone myapp --domain=staging.myapp.com --no-db --domain Required. Primary domain for the new app. --name Optional Linux username for the clone. --branch Deploy branch for the clone (defaults to the source app's branch). --env Environment label for the clone (since v5.8.0 ; defaults to the source app's). --env=staging writes APP_ENV=staging / CIPI_ENV=staging into the clone's .env and makes it read

The panel already had cipi api fix-permissions and cipi gui fix-permissions ; apps did not. A blunt chown -R app:app /home/<app> is wrong: nginx writes vhost logs as www-data into logs/ ( 2775 setgid), the home must stay 750 so www-data (in the app group) can read the docroot, .ssh must be 700 or OpenSSH StrictModes refuses the deploy key, and shared/.env is 640 . This command reapplies that layout — ownership of the tree except logs/ , then the log/ACL helper, storage dirs 775 , Composer auth.json 640 , cipi-databases.env 600 . One named app, or every app. cipi app fix-permissions myapp cipi app fix-permissions # every app on this server cipi deploy already runs the log-ACL helper before Deployer. fix-permissions is the full home, on demand, after someone unpacked a zip as root or chmod'd .ssh to 775. Available since v5.2.1 . No migration: cipi self-update copies the libs and refreshes shell completion. The panel sudoers file lists the new command, and since API 1.31 the panel calls it ( POST /api/apps/{name}/fix-permissions , and a button in the GUI ); existing servers pick that line up the next time sudoers is rewritten (the CLI runs as root and does not need it).

d: Read and change an app's .env safely.
x: Every Laravel app has a single .env file living at /home/<app>/shared/.env . Custom apps have no .env . It is created and pre-populated by Cipi during app create with the database credentials, APP_KEY , APP_URL , cache/session/queue settings, and the webhook token. The shared/ directory is symlinked into every release, so the same .env is always active regardless of which release is current. Edit interactively via CLI The safest way to change ENV values is through Cipi itself — it opens the file in nano as the app user, with the correct permissions: cipi app env myapp Save with Ctrl+O then exi

The safest way to change ENV values is through Cipi itself — it opens the file in nano as the app user, with the correct permissions: cipi app env myapp Save with Ctrl+O then exit with Ctrl+X . Changes take effect immediately for new requests — no restart needed for most values. If you change queue connection or cache driver, restart the workers: cipi worker restart myapp

Since v5.0.3 , scripts, the panel API, and the web GUI can manage .env without opening an editor: cipi app env myapp --show cipi app env myapp --show --json cipi app env myapp --get=APP_URL cipi app env myapp --set=APP_DEBUG=false cipi app env myapp --unset=LEGACY_KEY REST: GET|PUT /api/apps/{name}/env (ability apps-env , API 1.14+ ). MCP: AppEnvShow , AppEnvUpdate .
You can also edit the file directly over SSH as root or as the app user: # as root nano /home/myapp/shared/.env # or switch to the app user first su - myapp nano ~/shared/.env

d: Supervisor workers and Laravel Horizon per app.
x: Every app gets a default Supervisor worker for the default queue. You can add additional queues with custom process counts and timeouts. cipi worker add myapp --queue=emails --processes=3 cipi worker add myapp --queue=exports --processes=1 --timeout=7200 cipi worker list myapp cipi worker edit myapp --queue=default --processes=3 cipi worker remove myapp emails cipi worker restart myapp # restart all workers for the app cipi worker stop myapp # stop all workers for the app (used during deploys) # Laravel Horizon (v5.0+) — mutually exclusive with queue:work workers cipi worker horizon enable mya

Installing laravel/horizon used to change nothing until someone ran cipi worker horizon enable : the package was there and nothing processed the jobs. cipi deploy now looks at the release it has just published: What the deploy finds What it does laravel/horizon installed, QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis in the app's .env , no queue worker configured Enables Horizon, as cipi worker horizon enable would. Horizon installed, queue:work workers already configured Says how to hand the queues to Horizon. The workers stay as they are. Horizon installed, another queue connection (or none) Says which variable to set and the two commands to run. Nothing is changed. The .env is never edited : the queue connection is the app's decision. The advice is given once per situation, not at every deploy. cipi worker horizon disable is remembered: a Horizon you turned off is not turned back on by the next deploy. enable forgets it. A deploy started by a Git push runs as the app user and does not do this; cipi pending lists the apps left with Horizon installed, the queues on Redis and no worker. queue:restart still runs on every deploy: without workers it does nothing. On 5.0.x, cipi worker horizon enable could leave Horizon half enabled : the command printed nothing after “Enabling Horizon…” and status still said disabled . v5.1.0 fixes both causes, always writes the state, reports what Supervisor actually did, and makes status surface any drift between the two. If you hit this, run cipi self-update and enable it again. Queue workers can also be declared in the app's repository — see cipi.yml . Flag Desc

Each app user can restart, stop, or check workers without root — via a restricted sudo helper installed at /usr/local/bin/cipi-worker : # run as the app user (SSH or sudo su - myapp) sudo cipi-worker status myapp sudo cipi-worker stop myapp # used by Deployer before symlink swap sudo cipi-worker restart myapp As root, use cipi worker list|restart|stop <app> instead. There is no cipi worker status admin command — use cipi worker list or the app-user helper above.

Since v5.0 , manage the Laravel scheduler crontab entry that runs schedule:run (the crontab itself already existed; it is now toggleable and tracked in apps.json ). cipi schedule on myapp cipi schedule off myapp cipi schedule status myapp

Cipi automatically adds a crontab entry for the Laravel scheduler when an app is created: # installed automatically by cipi app create * * * * * /usr/bin/php8.5 /home/myapp/current/artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1 This entry runs as the myapp Linux user every minute, using the PHP version selected for the app. It is updated automatically when you change PHP version via cipi app edit myapp --php=X .
# as root — view the app user's crontab crontab -u myapp -l # or after switching to the app user su - myapp myapp@server:~$ crontab -l

You can add extra cron jobs to the app user's crontab. Switch to the app user first to ensure jobs run with the correct user context and file permissions: su - myapp myapp@server:~$ crontab -e Example entries you might add: # existing Laravel scheduler (do not remove) * * * * * /usr/bin/php8.5 /home/myapp/current/artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1 # nightly database backup at 2 AM 0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/cipi db backup myapp >> /home/myapp/logs/backup.log 2>&1 # custom script every 15 minutes */15 * * * * /home/myapp/current/scripts/sync.sh >> /home/myapp/logs/sync.log 2>&1 Do not remove the Laravel scheduler entry. Cipi does not re-add it automatically if deleted — you would need to run cipi app edit myapp --php=<current-version> to restore it. Always keep the schedule:run line as the first entry so it is easy to identify. Cron jobs run as the app user. They respect the same filesystem restrictions as the app itself. If a cron job needs to write files, make sure the target path is inside /home/myapp/ . Jobs that require root access should be added to the root crontab instead, with crontab -e as root.
# check system cron log grep CRON /var/log/syslog | grep myapp | tail -20 # check Laravel scheduler execution cipi app artisan myapp schedule:list

d: Enable Laravel Reverb behind Nginx for an app.
x: Laravel Reverb is Laravel's first-party WebSocket server. Cipi has run it since v5.0 ; v5.1.2 is the release that made it work in production — generated credentials, a scheme derived from the certificate, raised connection limits, and a proxy rule that no longer swallows your own routes. Enabling Reverb on a Laravel app wires four things: 127.0.0.1:9000–9099 A free localhost port, allocated per app and recorded in apps.json . Reverb never listens on a public interface. ${app}-reverb A Supervisor program running artisan reverb:start as the app user, logging to /home/<app>/logs/reverb.log . ngin

# 1. In the project, on your machine — require the package and the client side, # then commit. `install:broadcasting` writes resources/js/echo.js and config/reverb.php. composer require laravel/reverb php artisan install:broadcasting # 2. On the server — allocate the port, the Supervisor program and the nginx proxy. cipi app reverb enable myapp # 3. A certificate, so clients get wss:// instead of ws:// (skip if the app already has one). cipi ssl install myapp # 4. Deploy: composer install, the Node build, then Reverb starts on the new release. cipi deploy myapp cipi app reverb status myapp Order matters only in that the Node build has to run after reverb enable : Vite bakes VITE_REVERB_* into the bundle at build time. Cipi's node_build step runs after Deployer has linked the shared .env , so a deploy that follows enable produces a frontend that can find the socket. Change the domain or install a certificate later and you need another deploy for the bundle to catch up.

# Laravel Reverb — managed by Cipi (cipi app reverb status myapp) # Where the Supervisor program listens. Cipi owns this pair outright. REVERB_SERVER_HOST=127.0.0.1 REVERB_SERVER_PORT=9000 BROADCAST_CONNECTION=reverb # Generated once on the first enable, then never touched again. REVERB_APP_ID=482913 REVERB_APP_KEY=3f9c1ab27de40518b6c4 REVERB_APP_SECRET=a71f0e5c8d24b93a6f10c7e5482db9af # The public side — derived from what nginx actually serves. REVERB_HOST=myapp.com REVERB_PORT=443 REVERB_SCHEME=https # Read by Vite at build time and baked into the frontend bundle. VITE_REVERB_APP_KEY= "${REVERB_APP_KEY}" VITE_REVERB_HOST= "${REVERB_HOST}" VITE_REVERB_PORT= "${REVERB_PORT}" VITE_REVERB_SCHEME= "${REVERB_SCHEME}" Before 5.1.2 the three credentials were left blank for you to invent — and an empty REVERB_APP_KEY is exactly what stops reverb:start from booting. They are now generated on the first enable and an existing non-empty value always wins, so an app that arrived with its own credentials keeps them. Cipi never rotates them: a new key would disconnect every live client and invalidate any frontend bundle already built against the old one.

The stock resources/js/echo.js from install:broadcasting already reads exactly the variables Cipi writes — nothing to change: import Echo from 'laravel-echo' ; import Pusher from 'pusher-js' ; window.Pusher = Pusher; window.Echo = new Echo({ broadcaster: 'reverb' , key: import.meta.env.VITE_REVERB_APP_KEY, wsHost: import.meta.env.VITE_REVERB_HOST, wsPort: import.meta.env.VITE_REVERB_PORT ?? 80, wssPort: import.meta.env.VITE_REVERB_PORT ?? 443, forceTLS: (import.meta.env.VITE_REVERB_SCHEME ?? 'https' ) === 'https' , enabledTransports: [ 'ws' , 'wss' ], }); Because nginx fronts Reverb on the app's own domain and port, there is no extra port to open in the firewall and no second certificate to manage. cipi app reverb status prints the exact URL a client ends up dialling. /app and /apps belong to the protocol. Up to 5.1.1 the proxy was written as location /app , which in nginx is a prefix match, not a path — so on every app with Reverb enabled, /appointments , /apple and /application/… were proxied into Reverb instead of reaching Laravel. Since 5.1.2 the block is the regex ~ ^/apps?(/|$) , which matches only /app/{key} and /apps/{id}/… . An app that has its own /app or /apps route still cannot use Reverb behind the same domain — put it on a dedicated subdomain instead.

Cipi derives the public host, port and scheme from what the server actually serves rather than assuming HTTPS: no certificate http on port 80 — the app is served over HTTP, so the socket is ws:// . certificate present https on port 443 — wss:// . wildcard domain *.example.com resolves to a concrete host ( www.example.com ), because no browser can open a socket to a wildcard. A multi-tenant frontend has to pick its own host at runtime. Installing a certificate later — HTTP-01 or DNS-01 — moves the app's Reverb settings to wss:// on the spot, and a domain change re-derives them too. Before 5.1.2 these values were hardcoded to https /443 at enable time, which on an app without a certificate meant a browser silently refusing the connection as mixed content, with nothing in the Reverb log to explain it. reverb status now warns when the app has a certificate but the .env still says ws:// .

Every open WebSocket costs one file descriptor inside Reverb and two connections inside nginx, and the stock soft limit of 1024 stops an app at roughly a thousand concurrent clients — with nothing in any log to say why. Since 5.1.2 Cipi raises both ceilings: Supervisor A systemd drop-in at /etc/systemd/system/supervisor.service.d/cipi-nofile.conf setting LimitNOFILE=65535 , inherited by every program Supervisor runs. nginx worker_rlimit_nofile 65535 and worker_connections 8192 in nginx.conf , applied on a reload. nginx picks its new limits up on the reload Cipi performs. Supervisor picks its own up only on a restart , which also restarts every queue worker on the server — so Cipi configures the drop-in, tells you it is pending, and leaves the decision to you: systemctl restart supervisor # or, in one go, at enable time: cipi app reverb enable myapp --restart-supervisor The proxy read timeout was another silent limit: it used to be exactly Reverb's 60-second ping interval, so every idle client was a coin flip between the ping and the timeout. It now sits well clear of it, and Reverb's own ping/prune cycle is what reaps dead connections.

Reports the port, what Supervisor is doing with the process, the URL a client should be dialling, and the three failure modes that leave nothing in any log: cipi app reverb status myapp Reverb: enabled 127.0.0.1:9000 myapp-reverb RUNNING pid 21847, uptime 3 days, 4:12:07 Clients dial: wss://myapp.com:443/app/3f9c1ab27de40518b6c4 Open files: 65535 (supervisor) Missing in .env: … A credential is absent or empty — reverb:start will not boot. Re-run cipi app reverb enable . certificate but REVERB_SCHEME is 'http' The app gained a certificate after Reverb was enabled. Re-run enable to move it to wss:// , then deploy so the bundle catches up. default open-file limit The drop-in is in place but Supervisor has not been restarted, so the process is still capped near a thousand clients. The process log is /home/<app>/logs/reverb.log , and supervisorctl status myapp-reverb / restart myapp-reverb control the program directly.

cipi app reverb disable stops and removes the Supervisor program, regenerates the vhost without the proxy block, re-applies SSL, and — since 5.1.2 — points BROADCAST_CONNECTION back at whatever the app was broadcasting through before Reverb took over, falling back to log . Previously it left BROADCAST_CONNECTION=reverb behind, so every broadcast failed against a server that was no longer running. Only REVERB_SERVER_HOST and REVERB_SERVER_PORT are removed from the .env . The credentials stay: they are what a re-enable — or a frontend bundle already built against them — depends on.

cipi app clone used to copy the source's REVERB_* keys into the clone's .env — pointing a staging frontend at the production socket and handing it the production app secret — while never starting a Reverb for it. Since 5.1.2 a cloned Reverb app gets its own port, its own credentials and its own domain, the way it already got its own Octane. Reverb can also be declared in the project file with workers.reverb: true|false , planned and applied by cipi yml apply like Horizon and the queue workers, and emitted by cipi yml generate . Declaring it on a --custom app is refused up front. workers: horizon: false reverb: true # adds a Reverb WebSocket server to this app Upgrading from 5.0.x or 5.1.1? cipi self-update runs migration 5.1.2 , which raises both limits (and reports whether Supervisor still needs a restart), rewrites the vhost of every app whose Reverb location is still the greedy /app prefix — backed up to /var/lib/cipi/vhost-backup-5.1.2 , tested with nginx -t , SSL re-applied, and rolled back as a batch on failure — and fills in the missing .env keys without overwriting anything already there , so an app whose socket settings were tuned by hand keeps them. Re-deploy your Reverb apps afterwards so the frontend bundle picks up the VITE_REVERB_* values.

d: Cap CPU, memory and disk per app; suspend and resume apps.
x: cipi app limits Since v5.0 , set per-app resource limits with hard caps enforced by Cipi. cipi app limits myapp --fpm-max-children=20 --memory-limit=256M cipi app limits myapp --octane-workers=4 --worker-procs=3 cipi app limits myapp --disk=10 # soft disk limit in GB (v5.5.0+) — alerts, blocks nothing cipi app limits myapp --disk=none # back to no limit (the default) cipi app limits myapp # show current limits --fpm-max-children PHP-FPM pm.max_children for FPM apps. --memory-limit PHP memory_limit . --octane-workers Octane worker count for FrankenPHP apps. Since v5.10.0 , rewriting the Octane

Since v5.0 , set per-app resource limits with hard caps enforced by Cipi. cipi app limits myapp --fpm-max-children=20 --memory-limit=256M cipi app limits myapp --octane-workers=4 --worker-procs=3 cipi app limits myapp --disk=10 # soft disk limit in GB (v5.5.0+) — alerts, blocks nothing cipi app limits myapp --disk=none # back to no limit (the default) cipi app limits myapp # show current limits --fpm-max-children PHP-FPM pm.max_children for FPM apps. --memory-limit PHP memory_limit . --octane-workers Octane worker count for FrankenPHP apps. Since v5.10.0 , rewriting the Octane Supervisor program also applies its new environment: the app's own ini directory on PHP_INI_SCAN_DIR (where JIT lives) and /home/<app>/current first on PATH , so Octane finds the pinned binary. --worker-procs Supervisor queue worker process count. --disk Soft disk limit in GB for files and database together (e.g. 10 , 2.5 ), or none . Since v5.5.0 .

No app has a disk limit unless one is set: the default is unlimited, on new and existing servers alike. --disk sets one for the app's files and database together — the TOTAL column of cipi disk — and the command reports what the app uses now, warning if it is already over. It is soft. Nothing is blocked when the limit is passed and the app keeps working. The limit is a threshold for the app_disk monitor check: a warning at 90% of the limit, a critical alert once over it, a recovery when it is back under, with the usual reminder every 4 hours in between (trigger monitor_app_disk ). Setting only --disk does not rebuild the FPM pool or restart workers. cipi disk shows the limit next to the app ( 10 GB (64%) , and over once passed). The limit is stored next to the app as disk_limit_gb , not inside limits : that object is what cipi.yml reconciles, and an app's repository must not be able to raise the space its server grants it. cipi sync carries it with the app. Since API 1.32 the same reading and the same write are GET|PUT /api/apps/{name}/limits ( disk_limit_gb ; abilities apps-view / apps-edit ; null removes it). The PHP SDK calls limits() . The control panel shows the limit on Server → Disk (panel 3.1 / API 1.33) and sets it on the host. cipi-cli reads usage with disk and leaves the limit to this command.

Available since v4.5.8 . Take an app offline without deleting it — useful for billing holds, maintenance windows, or staging sites you want fully dark. Suspending swaps the Nginx vhost for a static HTTP 503 page served from /var/www/cipi-suspended/ . cipi app suspend myapp # take offline (503 page) cipi app unsuspend myapp # restore normal vhost Command Description cipi app suspend <app> Sets suspended: true in apps.json , rebuilds the vhost to return 503 for all requests. Idempotent if already suspended. cipi app unsuspend <app> Clears the flag, restores the normal Laravel/custom vhost, and reapplies SSL blocks. Idempotent if already online.

HTTPS included — certbot clones the suspension vhost into the :443 block, so HTTPS also shows the offline page Let's Encrypt still works — the /.well-known/acme-challenge/ path stays public so certificates can be issued or renewed while suspended Survives vhost regeneration — alias changes, PHP edits, and SSL installs respect the suspended flag Visible in listings — cipi app list marks suspended apps; cipi domains appends ⏸ suspended on each row Suspend vs basic auth: cipi basicauth shows a login prompt but still runs your app. app suspend stops PHP entirely and serves a static offline page — visitors never reach Laravel. Use suspend for “site closed”; basic auth for “invite-only preview”. Also available via the REST API ( POST /api/apps/{name}/suspend ), cipi-cli ( apps suspend ), and the WHMCS module (Suspend / Unsuspend buttons). Requires token ability apps-suspend for API access.

d: Password-protect an app behind HTTP basic auth.
x: Available since v4.5.2 . Protect any app — Laravel or custom — behind an Nginx username/password prompt. Useful for staging sites, internal tools, or apps that aren't ready for public traffic yet. Command Description cipi basicauth enable <app> [--user=NAME] [--password=PASS] Turn on HTTP basic auth. Credentials are generated when omitted and shown once on screen — save them immediately cipi basicauth disable <app> Remove the prompt and clear stored credentials cipi basicauth status <app> Show whether basic auth is enabled and the configured user Credentials are hashed with openssl passwd -apr

Editors, pagers, shells, and REPLs are blocked ( nano , vim , less , bash , tinker , …). Interactive flags (e.g. tail -f , php -a ) are rejected. cipi app run myapp composer install --no-dev cipi app run myapp npm ci cipi app run myapp ls -la shared cipi app run --commands # list allowed binaries cipi app run --commands --json Allowed binaries include composer , npm / npx / yarn / pnpm , ls / ll , cat / head / tail , filesystem helpers, archives, g

Editors, pagers, shells, and REPLs are blocked ( nano , vim , less , bash , tinker , …). Interactive flags (e.g. tail -f , php -a ) are rejected. cipi app run myapp composer install --no-dev cipi app run myapp npm ci cipi app run myapp ls -la shared cipi app run --commands # list allowed binaries cipi app run --commands --json Allowed binaries include composer , npm / npx / yarn / pnpm , ls / ll , cat / head / tail , filesystem helpers, archives, git , php , node , and find . REST: POST /api/apps/{name}/run (async job, ability apps-run ) and GET /api/run-commands (API 1.14+ ). MCP: AppRun , AppRunCommands . v5.0.4+ fixed /usr/bin/env: '--': No such file or directory — every whitelisted command (including GUI App commands) failed before that patch. Run cipi self-update .

Run Artisan commands and Tinker as the app user with the correct PHP version and open_basedir context — exactly as they would run during a deploy. cipi app artisan myapp migrate:status cipi app artisan myapp queue:retry all cipi app artisan myapp db:seed --class=ProductionSeeder cipi app artisan myapp cache:clear cipi app tinker myapp

Tail application logs in real-time. By default, all logs are shown, including the Laravel log in shared/storage/logs/ . Logs are rotated daily by logrotate and kept according to the retention policy . cipi app logs myapp # all logs (incl. the Laravel log) cipi app logs myapp --type=nginx # Nginx access + error cipi app logs myapp --type=php # PHP-FPM errors cipi app logs myapp --type=worker # queue worker output cipi app logs myapp --type=deploy # deploy history cipi app logs myapp --type=laravel # Laravel application logs --type=nginx Nginx access and error logs --type=php PHP-FPM error log --type=worker Supervisor / queue worker output --type=deploy Deployer output — full deploy history with timestamps --type=laravel Laravel application logs from shared/storage/logs/ ( laravel.log since v5.5.0)

Up to 5.4, cipi app create wrote LOG_CHANNEL=daily into every Laravel app's .env , so Laravel wrote one file per day ( laravel-2026-09-24.log ) — and the cipi-app-logs logrotate rule then rotated each of those files once more, a day or two later. The content moved to laravel-<date>.log.1 , which was never compressed and never deleted, so the 12-month retention did not apply to Laravel logs; and the empty laravel-<date>.log left behind is the file cipi app logs --type=laravel and the panel read, so the log looked empty while the entries sat next to it. Since v5.5.0 apps log to a single storage/logs/laravel.log , and logrotate alone rotates it: daily, compressed from the second day, 365 rotations. New apps get LOG_CHANNEL=single in shared/.env . Existing apps are switched by the 5.5.0 migration , which also folds the dated files into laravel.log . The logrotate pattern is now storage/logs/*[!0-9].log , which leaves out any log whose name ends in a date. An app that sets LOG_CHANNEL=daily again on purpose gets what Laravel does by itself: one file per day, pruned after LOG_DAILY_DAYS . Every other .log in storage/logs is rotated as before.

d: SFTP and SSH access for each app's own Linux user.
x: Each app runs under its own isolated Linux user. Sometimes you need to work directly inside that user's environment — inspect files, run one-off scripts, or debug something that only reproduces as the correct user. Direct SSH as app user (recommended) App users can SSH directly to the server with the password generated at app creation: # connect as the app user (password auth) ssh myapp@your-server-ip # you are directly inside the app user's shell myapp@server:~$ pwd /home/myapp myapp@server:~$ cd ~/current myapp@server:~$ ls The password is shown when the app is created (or use cipi app reset

App users can SSH directly to the server with the password generated at app creation: # connect as the app user (password auth) ssh myapp@your-server-ip # you are directly inside the app user's shell myapp@server:~$ pwd /home/myapp myapp@server:~$ cd ~/current myapp@server:~$ ls The password is shown when the app is created (or use cipi app reset-password myapp to regenerate it). This works for SFTP clients, IDE remote sessions, and terminal access. Since v5.5.0 this access can be turned off from outside the server, for one app ( cipi ssh apps disable myapp ) or for all of them, including the apps created later ( cipi ssh apps disable --all ). Deploys keep working, because Deployer reaches the app user over ssh localhost , and the admin path below is unaffected. See cipi ssh apps .

If you are already connected as cipi , become root with su root (root password from the installation summary — sudo only runs cipi itself) and switch to any app user: ssh cipi@your-server-ip cipi@server:~$ su root root@server:~# su - myapp myapp@server:~$ pwd /home/myapp
If you need to regenerate an app user's password (e.g. for direct SSH or SFTP), use: cipi app reset-password myapp The new password is displayed on screen — save it immediately.

h: Useful commands once logged in as the app user
x: # navigate to the active release myapp@server:~$ cd ~/current # run artisan directly with the correct PHP version myapp@server:~$ /usr/bin/php8.5 ~/current/artisan tinker # inspect the shared .env myapp@server:~$ cat ~/shared/.env # tail all logs myapp@server:~$ tail -f ~/logs/*.log # check active releases (ll is a built-in alias for ls -al) myapp@server:~$ ll ~/releases/ Every app user's .bashrc defines a handy ll='ls -al' alias (since v4.5.5 ) for quicker directory listings over SSH, alongside the deploy and composer shortcuts. Apps created before 4.5.5 receive the ll alias automatically on the next cipi self-update via the 4.5.5 migration . The app user's open_basedir restriction limits PHP to /home/myapp . This is enforced at the PHP-FPM level, not at the shell level — you can access any file your shell user can read when working in the terminal.

d: The deploy paths Cipi supports and when to use each.
x: With Cipi, CI (build and test) and CD (release to production) can be split or combined. Every deploy ultimately runs the same Deployer pipeline on the server — clone, composer install , migrations, symlink swap, worker restart. What changes is what triggers that pipeline. Cipi supports two trigger models. For most Laravel apps, start with the webhook + Cipi Agent path. Move to a full CI/CD pipeline when you need gates, backups, or infrastructure orchestration that a simple push hook cannot express. Two ways to trigger a deploy Webhook + Cipi Agent (recommended) CI/CD pipeline via SSH Trigger G

Use case Recommended approach Where to read more Single Laravel app, push-to-deploy on main Webhook + Agent Webhook setup Deploy only if CI tests pass Pipeline SSH (disable production webhook) Pipeline SSH deploy DB + file backup before every production release Pipeline SSH Safe deploy w/ backup Slack / Telegram alerts on deploy outcome Pipeline SSH Deploy notifications Ephemeral URL per feature branch (review apps) Pipeline SSH Preview environments Deploy multiple apps on one server from one repo Either — webhook per app, or one pipeline with parallel cipi deploy Multi-app deploy Pick one trigger per app. Do not leave a production webhook active while also running pipeline deploys on push — two concurrent Deployer runs conflict on the lock file. Use cipi deploy myapp --unlock if a stuck lock is left behind.

d: cipi deploy, releases, rollback, status and logs.
x: Cipi uses Deployer for all deployments. Every deploy is atomic: a new release directory is prepared fully before the current symlink is swapped, so traffic is never interrupted. $ cipi deploy shop $ cipi deploy shop --releases $ cipi deploy shop --rollback Since v4.5.4 Cipi bundles Deployer 8 , which requires PHP ≥ 8.3 . cipi deploy and cipi deploy --rollback abort with a clear upgrade message before invoking Deployer when an app is still pinned to an older PHP version — switch it with cipi app edit <app> --php=8.3 (or higher) first. Deployer version (v5.10.0+) Up to 5.9.x the installer downlo

Up to 5.9.x the installer downloaded https://deployer.org/deployer.phar , which now serves Deployer 6.8.0 : no deploy:publish , so every deploy of a fresh server stopped at Task `deploy:publish` not found ( #519 ). Since v5.10.0 Deployer comes from its GitHub release, pinned to 8.0.5 , checked against the SHA-256 GitHub publishes for deployer.phar and asked its version before it is installed; setup.sh stops when it cannot install it, and cipi deploy refuses Deployer 6 with what to run. Migration 5.10.0 moves a server on Deployer 6 or 7 to 8.0.5 — keeping 7, and naming the apps, where an app still runs PHP below 8.3. dep --version # Deployer 8.0.5 # by hand, as root (what setup.sh and the migration run) source /opt/cipi/lib/deployer-install.sh && cipi_deployer_install

Deployer and Composer run with the app's configured PHP version (e.g. /usr/bin/php8.5 ), not the system default. This applies to cipi deploy , cipi deploy --rollback , crontab deploy triggers, cipi sync import deploys, and the deploy / composer aliases in the app user's .bashrc . Stop queue workers ( cipi worker stop ) Clone repo into releases/N/ Run composer install --no-dev (with app's PHP) Link shared/.env and shared/storage/ Run artisan migrate --force Run artisan optimize Run artisan storage:link Swap current symlink atomically Restart queue workers Prune old releases (keep last 5) cipi deploy myapp # deploy latest commit cipi deploy myapp --rollback # instant rollback to previous release cipi deploy myapp --releases # list releases with date, how long the deploy took (v5.7.2+), commit and subject cipi deploy myapp --history # v5.9.0+ past deploys and rollbacks: result, release, duration, who started it [--limit=30] [--json] cipi deploy --last # v5.9.0+ the last deploy of every app [--json] cipi deploy myapp --log # timestamped deploy log (v5.1.0+) cipi deploy myapp --log=200 # last 200 lines of it cipi deploy myapp --status # v5.8.4+ is a deploy running right now, whoever started it? [--json] [--tail=N] cipi deploy myapp --audit # v5.4.0+ who and what deployed each release [--days=90] [--json] cipi deploy myapp --key # show the SSH deploy key cipi deploy myapp --webhook # show webhook URL and token cipi deploy myapp --unlock # remove a stuck deploy lock (a failed deploy releases its own since v5.9.0) cipi deploy myapp --snapshot # v5.0+ opt-in DB dump before deploy ci

Up to 5.0.x a failing deploy could pass in silence: the failure branch, its warnings, the rollback hint and the deploy_fail email were unreachable code, because a non-zero exit from Deployer killed the cipi process on the spot. Since v5.1.0 : Both paths email on success and on failure — the CLI and the automatic Git webhook alike. Subjects are visibly different ( Cipi deploy succeeded: myapp release 55 … / Cipi deploy FAILED: myapp … ), and the body names the branch, the release number, the commit hash and subject, its author and date, the duration, the previous release, the deploy log path and the post-deploy healthcheck verdict. cipi deploy exits non-zero when the deploy failed , so CI and webhooks can see it. The same applies to cipi deploy --rollback . The success email is sent after post-deploy verification , so it can never announce a successful deploy while the site is returning 500.

/home/<app>/logs/deploy.log used to be raw Deployer output appended forever, which made a deploy that failed overnight unreadable afterwards. Since v5.1.0 every line is timestamped and each run is bracketed by a banner naming the trigger (CLI or webhook), the branch, the release and the duration. cipi deploy myapp --log=100 # same as tailing /home/myapp/logs/deploy.log cipi deploy myapp --releases # release number, date, TOOK (5.7.2+), commit, subject Release directories stay numeric — rollback depends on that ordering — so --releases adds the human detail on top rather than renaming anything. Since v5.0 , opt-in pre-deploy DB snapshots are available via --snapshot / --snapshot-required or a permanent app setting — see Pre-deploy DB snapshots . Octane apps use the laravel-octane.php Deployer template (reload/restart Octane on deploy); enable Node builds with cipi app edit <app> --node-build='…' . Since v5.9.0 a deploy that fails releases its own lock: the next one starts without --unlock (the Laravel recipes end with after('deploy:failed', 'deploy:unlock') , and the update adds the line to the deploy.php of existing apps). A lock is still left behind when a deploy is interrupted — the process killed, the server restarted: use cipi deploy myapp --unlock to remove it before re-deploying. Not sure whether it is interrupted or still working? cipi deploy myapp --status (v5.8.4+) tells the two apart.

A deploy started by a Git push has nobody watching it. cipi deploy <app> --status answers from what both deploy paths already write — the start and end banners of /home/<app>/logs/deploy.log — and from the processes still alive, so it covers cipi deploy , the panel, the webhook, cipi/agent and rollbacks alike. It is read-only and safe to poll; the panel does, to show a deploy it did not start. cipi deploy myapp --status cipi deploy myapp --status --json --tail=20 # for scripts and the panel API, with the last 20 log lines State Meaning running A start banner with no end yet and a process still on it. phase is deploy while Deployer builds the release, post-deploy while the post-deploy steps, cipi.yml and the healthcheck run after it. current names the trigger ( cli , panel , webhook , mcp , rollback ), the branch, the previous release, the start time and the seconds elapsed. queued The webhook has received a push and the per-minute cron has not started the deploy yet. interrupted A start banner with no end and nothing alive any more — a reboot, a kill. The lock it left behind is what --unlock removes. idle Nothing running. last says how the previous run ended: result, kind (deploy or rollback), release, duration, exit code, trigger.

h: Past deploys, and how long each took (v5.9.0+)
x: Both deploy paths end a run with a banner in the deploy log — result, release, duration, exit code. The log is rotated every night, so the banner of yesterday's deploy is no longer in deploy.log but in deploy.log.1 , and after that in a .gz . Anything that read the current file alone — the panel did — showed how long a deploy took until the first night and never again: a deploy you start is watched while it runs, one a Git push starts is looked at the day after. --history reads the rotated files too. cipi deploy myapp --history # newest first: finished, result, release, took, trigger, branch cipi deploy myapp --history --limit=100 --json cipi deploy --last # every app: when it was last deployed and how it went cipi deploy --last --json # what the app list of the panel shows A run is a deploy or a rollback, ok or failed , with its release, its duration in seconds, its exit code, what started it ( cli , panel , webhook , mcp , rollback ), the branch and the release it replaced. Times are ISO 8601 with the server's offset. The keys are those of last in --status --json . Files are read newest first and only as far back as it takes; a run that starts before a rotation and ends after it keeps its start. cipi deploy myapp --releases finds the duration of a release in the rotated logs as well. Scripts that cannot be sure of the Cipi version put the flag first: cipi deploy --history myapp . A Cipi older than 5.9.0 takes the flag for an app name and answers not found ; cipi deploy myapp --history on it would start a deploy. The panel API uses the first form.
