d: Tenant subdomains with a wildcard certificate.
x: Yes, Cipi does wildcards — one app answering on every <tenant>.myapp.com , with one certificate that covers all of them. It takes two separate things, and most problems come from having only one of them: Routing — Nginx sends *.myapp.com to the app when the pattern is one of its names: cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com' (or a wildcard primary domain). Works since v5.1.0 , whatever DNS or certificate you use. Certificate — Let's Encrypt validates a wildcard name over DNS-01 only : it asks for a TXT record in the zone. Cipi creates that record through the Cloudflare API , the only DNS provider i

DNS of the zone Wildcard certificate Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode Commands Cloudflare, proxied (orange cloud) — recommended for a SaaS Let's Encrypt over DNS-01 (proxy can stay on) — or Cloudflare Origin CA Full (strict) steps below Cloudflare, DNS only (grey cloud) Let's Encrypt over DNS-01 not used (traffic does not go through Cloudflare) steps below , skip the SSL/TLS mode Another DNS provider not by Cipi — move the DNS to Cloudflare (free), list the subdomains, or bring your own certificate — without Cloudflare Cloudflare Tunnel ( cipi zt hostname add ) not needed: Cloudflare terminates HTTPS, the tunnel talks HTTP to :80 set by the tunnel cipi zt

DNS records in the Cloudflare dashboard: A @ → <server-ip> and A * → <server-ip> ( AAAA too if the server has IPv6). The * record also covers www , app , admin … unless a record with that exact name exists. Proxied or DNS only: both work, wildcard records can be proxied on every plan. API token — Cloudflare → My Profile → API Tokens → Create Token → template Edit zone DNS , Zone Resources: Include → Specific zone → myapp.com . The only permission needed is Zone → DNS → Edit . Give it to Cipi , once per server (several accounts: --name= ). Route the subdomains to the app with a wildcard alias. Quote it, so the shell does not expand the * . Issue the certificate over DNS-01. Cipi asks for myapp.com + *.myapp.com + any other alias the wildcard does not cover, writes the HTTPS vhost and redirects every subdomain from HTTP to HTTPS. It takes about a minute (Cipi waits 30 seconds for the TXT record to propagate). Proxied records only: Cloudflare → SSL/TLS → Overview → Full (strict) . Also check Rules → Configuration Rules / Page Rules: a rule that sets SSL to Flexible for a hostname wins over the global setting. Check — cipi ssl status lists every app with the certificate it is served with and the names that certificate does not cover. cipi ssl dns set --token=YOUR_CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN # step 3 cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com' # step 4 cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare # step 5 cipi ssl status # step 7 curl -sI https://tenant1.myapp.com | head -1 # HTTP/2 200 (or your app's answer) Renewals need nothing: each certificate renews the way it was issued (certbot.timer twice a day

h: Cloudflare proxy: the SSL/TLS mode decides everything
x: With the orange cloud, the visitor talks HTTPS to Cloudflare, and Cloudflare opens a second connection to your server. The SSL/TLS mode says how: Flexible — never with Cipi. Cloudflare connects to http:// on port 80. As soon as the app has a certificate, Cipi answers port 80 with a redirect to HTTPS, which Cloudflare fetches again over HTTP: an endless loop ( ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS ). Without a certificate it "works", but Laravel sees plain HTTP and builds http:// URLs. Full — Cloudflare connects over HTTPS and accepts any certificate. Works, but does not protect the second hop. Full (strict) — HTTPS with a valid certificate for the hostname: the Let's Encrypt certificate from Cipi, or a Cloudflare Origin CA one. The right setting. Order for a new site behind the proxy: issue the certificate first with --dns=cloudflare (DNS-01 does not care about the proxy, the firewall or port 80), then switch to Full (strict). HTTP-01 behind the proxy depends on Cloudflare settings (Always Use HTTPS, WAF rules, Under Attack mode, cipi zt lock http ) — you do not need to turn the proxy off and on again if you use DNS-01. The edge certificate Cloudflare shows to visitors (Universal SSL, free) covers myapp.com and *.myapp.com : one level of subdomains. Deeper names ( a.b.myapp.com ) need Cloudflare's Advanced Certificate Manager at the edge, and their own wildcard at the origin. You see What it means on a Cipi server Fix ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS SSL/TLS mode Flexible (or a Configuration Rule setting it for that host) Full (strict) 525 SSL handshake failed No app on the server has that hostname

h: Alternative behind the proxy: Cloudflare Origin CA
x: A certificate signed by Cloudflare, valid 15 years, trusted only by Cloudflare : fine for proxied records with Full (strict), a browser warning for a DNS-only record. It covers the app's names, wildcard alias included. It needs the cipi zt API token (Zone → SSL and Certificates → Edit), not the DNS-01 one. Since 5.5.1 it works on an app that never had HTTPS, and survives every vhost change. cipi zt token set --token=ZT_TOKEN --account=ACCOUNT_ID cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com' cipi zt origin-cert myapp # reissue after adding names

When the zone is hosted elsewhere, Cipi cannot create the TXT record, so it cannot issue a wildcard certificate. Routing still works ( cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com' plus a * record at your provider), but HTTPS needs one of these: Move the DNS to Cloudflare (recommended) — free plan, records set to DNS only : traffic does not change, only who answers DNS. Then follow the Cloudflare steps and skip the SSL/TLS mode. List the subdomains — when tenants are few and known, add each one as an alias (no wildcard) and let HTTP-01 issue one certificate for all of them: cipi alias add myapp acme.myapp.com , then cipi ssl install myapp . Every name needs its own DNS record (or the * record), port 80 must be reachable, a certificate holds at most 100 names, and every reissue counts toward Let's Encrypt's limit of 50 certificates per domain per week — not a fit for self-service signup. Bring your own certificate — issue it with the certbot DNS plugin of your provider (Route 53, DigitalOcean, OVH, Gandi, …) under the certificate name Cipi expects : the app's primary domain (without *. for a wildcard primary). Cipi finds it in /etc/letsencrypt/live/<name>/ and serves it; certbot renews it with your plugin and Cipi's hook reloads nginx. Do not run cipi ssl install on that app afterwards: without --dns=cloudflare it reissues over HTTP-01, without the wildcard. # option 3, example with Route 53 (credentials as the plugin documents them) apt install python3-certbot-dns-route53 certbot certonly --dns-route53 -d myapp.com -d '*.myapp.com' --cert-name myapp.com cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.c

Other apps still win on their exact names. With *.myapp.com on one app, api.myapp.com can still be a separate app: Nginx prefers an exact server_name to a wildcard. Unknown hosts are closed by cipi nginx default-server (on by default) instead of reaching your tenant resolver. Laravel : set SESSION_DOMAIN=.myapp.com only if a login must be shared across subdomains; resolve the tenant from the Host header. APP_URL is set to https://www.myapp.com for a wildcard primary. Depth : Nginx's *.myapp.com also matches a.b.myapp.com , certificates do not — keep tenants one label deep. One app per tenant is the alternative when tenants need isolation (own database, own backups, movable to another server): create each tenant as its own Cipi app with its exact domain through the Cipi API , and its DNS record through the Cloudflare API — every tenant then gets a plain HTTP-01 certificate.

d: Nginx redirects and prefix reverse proxies per app.
x: cipi redirect Available since v5.3.1 . Two kinds of redirect, both stored in apps.json ( redirect and redirects[] ) and rendered by the same vhost generator as everything else. They survive every vhost regeneration — alias, www, basic auth, PHP switch, cipi sync import — and certbot clones them into :443 like any other location. # The whole app moved: every name, www included, in one hop cipi redirect set oldsite --to=https://new.com # 301, path and query kept cipi redirect set oldsite --to=https://new.com --302 --no-path cipi redirect disable oldsite # serve the app again, keep the target cip

Available since v5.3.1 . Two kinds of redirect, both stored in apps.json ( redirect and redirects[] ) and rendered by the same vhost generator as everything else. They survive every vhost regeneration — alias, www, basic auth, PHP switch, cipi sync import — and certbot clones them into :443 like any other location. # The whole app moved: every name, www included, in one hop cipi redirect set oldsite --to=https://new.com # 301, path and query kept cipi redirect set oldsite --to=https://new.com --302 --no-path cipi redirect disable oldsite # serve the app again, keep the target cipi redirect enable oldsite cipi redirect unset oldsite # forget it # Path redirects cipi redirect add myapp /old-pricing /pricing # exact, same app cipi redirect add myapp /blog/ https://blog.example.com/ # prefix cipi redirect add myapp /docs/ https://docs.example.com --308 --no-path cipi redirect list myapp [--json] cipi redirect remove myapp /old-pricing

cipi redirect set <app> --to=<url> sends every name the app answers to — primary domain, aliases and the www host — to the target in a single hop. The path and query are kept by default ( old.com/a?b → https://new.com/a?b ); --no-path sends everything to the target as is. The status is --301 (default), --302 , --307 or --308 . The ACME challenge stays public, so the old name's certificate keeps renewing and HTTPS visitors still get a valid redirect. A target served by the app itself is refused: it would loop. enable / disable toggle the saved target without losing it; unset removes it.

cipi redirect add <app> <from> <to> . <to> is a same-app /path or an http(s):// URL. Adding an existing <from> updates it. <from> Matches Example No trailing / Exact path. Only the query string is carried over, unless <to> has its own. /old?x=1 → /new?x=1 Trailing / Prefix. The rest of the raw request URI is appended; /blog without the slash goes to the target too. /blog/x?y → https://blog.example.com/x?y Either, with --no-path Everything goes to <to> unchanged. /blog/x → https://blog.example.com/ Path redirects and proxy prefixes keep working while the app redirect is on: they are more specific than location / , so a site that moved can keep /api/ where it was.

Paths and URLs outside a safe charset — no quotes, $ , ; , braces or whitespace — so a rule cannot inject nginx directives. Write source paths decoded : nginx matches the decoded URI. / , the ACME challenge, /favicon.ico , /robots.txt , /index.php , /cipi/webhook , and /app / /apps on a Reverb app. A path another redirect or proxy already occupies — for example a redirect and a proxy both on /api/ . A redirect that would loop back into itself. Safe apply. nginx -t must pass before the change. If nginx refuses the new vhost, apps.json and the vhost are restored and the command exits 1. cipi app show lists the app redirect and path redirects; changes fire the redirect_change notification (on by default). Since Cipi 5.4.1 the panel API ( 1.31+ ) and the GUI can manage redirects too, with the CLI's own validation; an app can also declare them in cipi.yml .

Available since v5.3.1 . Hand one URL prefix of an app to another HTTP service — a Node or Go API, a legacy app, a docs site — with location ^~ <prefix> and proxy_pass . Stored in apps.json ( proxies[] ), so it survives vhost regeneration like redirects do. cipi proxy add myapp /api/ http://127.0.0.1:3000 --strip-prefix cipi proxy add myapp /events/ http://127.0.0.1:4000 --no-buffering --timeout=3600 cipi proxy add myapp /docs/ https://docs-origin.example.com --preserve-host cipi proxy list myapp [--json] cipi proxy remove myapp /api/ Option Effect (none) The URI goes upstream unchanged: /api/users → <upstream>/api/users . --strip-prefix /api/users → <upstream>/users , and X-Forwarded-Prefix is sent. Required when the upstream has a path ( http://h/v1 ), because such an upstream always replaces the prefix. --preserve-host Send the visitor's Host . By default Host is the upstream's. --timeout=60 Upstream timeout in seconds. --no-buffering For Server-Sent Events, long polling and streamed downloads. --force Skip the loopback guard (below). Every proxy gets WebSocket upgrade, X-Real-IP , X-Forwarded-For , X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host , plus proxy_ssl_server_name for HTTPS upstreams. When basic auth is on, it covers the prefix too. Prefixes follow the same validation and reserved paths as path redirects , and keep working while an app redirect is on.

A proxy to 127.0.0.1 or localhost on a port Cipi already uses is refused without --force : nginx itself (80/443), SSH, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Valkey, Meilisearch, and any app's Octane or Reverb port. An upstream hostname that does not resolve is refused, since nginx resolves it at reload; one that does not answer within 5 seconds is only a warning. As with redirects, nginx -t must pass or apps.json and the vhost are restored and the command exits 1. cipi app show lists the proxy prefixes, and changes fire proxy_change (on by default). See also cipi help proxy . Since Cipi 5.4.1 , the panel API ( 1.31+ ) and the GUI can add, list and remove proxies — always without --force , so the loopback guard cannot be bypassed from the web. Proxies declared in cipi.yml are stricter still: link-local and 0.0.0.0/8 upstreams, cloud metadata included, are refused, and resolved hostnames are checked as well as literal IPs.

d: The default server and editing an app's Nginx config.
x: cipi nginx default-server Available since v5.1.0 . Claims whichever of :80 / :443 has no default server and closes unmatched requests with an empty reply ( 444 ). cipi nginx default-server status cipi nginx default-server on cipi nginx default-server off Cipi always had a default server on :80 , but never on :443 . An HTTPS request carrying an unknown Host therefore fell through to whichever vhost Nginx had loaded first — for a wildcard multi-tenant app, straight into a tenant resolver that cannot parse it. It is enabled on fresh installs, and migration 5.1.0 claims it on existing servers wher

Available since v5.1.0 . Claims whichever of :80 / :443 has no default server and closes unmatched requests with an empty reply ( 444 ). cipi nginx default-server status cipi nginx default-server on cipi nginx default-server off Cipi always had a default server on :80 , but never on :443 . An HTTPS request carrying an unknown Host therefore fell through to whichever vhost Nginx had loaded first — for a wildcard multi-tenant app, straight into a tenant resolver that cannot parse it. It is enabled on fresh installs, and migration 5.1.0 claims it on existing servers where nothing else already does. If another vhost legitimately owns the default server, the command says so and changes nothing.

Nginx is on the unattended-upgrades blacklist, so patches are applied when you ask for them: cipi nginx upgrade [--yes] runs apt --only-upgrade over the installed nginx* packages, keeps your nginx.conf , checks the config with nginx -t and reloads. Since v5.9.0 the nightly cipi autoupdate runs the same code. Details in manual stack upgrades .

nginx 1.31.9 (18 November 2026) is a security release with ten CVEs. Cipi 5.9.1 brings every server to it; cipi self-update is all it takes. What applies to a Cipi server: CVE-2026-118899 — an endless loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3: one request keeps a worker at 100% CPU. Any HTTPS vhost, so every server . CVE-2026-125283 — a buffer overflow with try_files under an alias . The panel API vhost had exactly that for /api-docs ; 5.9.1 serves it without the alias , which did nothing, and the migration removes the line from an installed vhost. CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 — memory corruption in the HTTP/2 code. Cipi 4 and 5 write listen 443 ssl; , never http2 on; , and nginx has HTTP/2 off by default since 1.25.1, so a server as Cipi sets it up cannot be reached by either. They apply where HTTP/2 was turned on by hand, on a vhost written by Cipi 3, or by an older version of the preview environments workflow on this site, which added listen 443 ssl http2; . The other six are in parts Cipi does not use: the resolver, HTTP/3, mail, stream and the PROXY protocol v2. cipi nginx security # patch level, the binary that is running, where HTTP/2 is on It prints the installed version against the oldest one that carries every fix Cipi knows about (1.31.9), whether the nginx that answers requests is the one on disk, and every configuration file that turns HTTP/2 on. It only reports; cipi pending carries the first two as items (below 1.31.9, the archive's build, an old binary still running). Which nginx a server runs. Since 4.5.9 Cipi runs nginx from nginx.org's mainlin
To customise the Nginx vhost for an app, edit the site config directly. After changes, test and reload Nginx. sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/<app> sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

Migration 5.6.3 moves existing servers off the PPA, removing it only once sury.org is in place. $ cipi php list $ cipi php install 8.3 $ cipi app edit blog --php=8.5 Since v4.5.4 Cipi bundles Deployer 8 (since v5.10.0 pinned to 8.0.5 from its GitHub release and checked against its SHA-256 — see Deployer version ), which requires PHP ≥ 8.3 . cipi php install , cipi php switch , cipi app create and cipi app edit therefore accept only 8.3, 8.4, 8.5 and, since v5.9.1 , 8.6 . Legacy versions (7.4–8.2) remain detectable and removable, so you can still clean up a pre-4.5.4 server with cipi php remove <old-version> . A server installed before v4.5.4 can still have PHP 7.4–8.2, with apps on them. Cipi manages what is there and adds nothing to it: cipi php list shows those versions (8.1 and older marked END OF LIFE), cipi service lists and restarts their FPM, and an app on one keeps it and keeps running. Since v5.9.1 cipi status lists their FPM t

A new server is installed with PHP 8.6. It is the server's PHP — the php command, the panel's pools — and what cipi app create uses when no --php is given. The installer does that when the repository has a release of 8.6 with every extension Cipi installs. While it only has a release candidate, or no redis , memcached or imagick package for 8.6 yet, the server gets 8.5 as before and the installer's last screen says why. That was still the case on the afternoon of 19 November 2026, the day PHP 8.6.0 was released: packages.sury.org had 8.6.0 itself and none of those three, so a server installed then got 8.5. The installer looks again at every install; nothing has to be updated for it to choose 8.6. On a server that got 8.5, cipi php install 8.6 and then cipi php switch 8.6 move it later. A server that is already installed keeps the PHP it has. Updating to 5.9.1 does not install 8.6, does not move an app to it and does not change the server's PHP. There 8.6 is a version you add: cipi php install 8.6 installs it next to the ones already there, and cipi php switch , cipi app create --php=8.6 , cipi app edit <app> --php=8.6 and php: "8.6" in cipi.yml accept it. Installing it does not make it the default: cipi app create without --php keeps using the server's PHP until cipi php switch 8.6 . When you install it while the branch is new, three things are worth knowing: You get what the repository has that day. PHP 8.6.0 was released on 19 November 2026 and packages.sury.org had it within hours; the Launchpad PPA, which servers set up before 5.6.3 may still use, carried a release cand

Since v4.7.13 , PHP packages are excluded from unattended-upgrades and managed by Cipi instead. cipi php upgrade runs apt-get update and --only-upgrade on every installed php* and libphp* package, then restarts the affected PHP-FPM pools. When SMTP is configured and packages were upgraded, Cipi sends an email ( php_upgrade trigger; disable with cipi notifications disable php_upgrade ). The check runs automatically every day at 03:30 via root crontab (wrapped by cipi-cron-notify ). Log: /var/log/cipi/php-upgrade.log . With nothing to upgrade, a run costs one apt-get update and restarts nothing. Migration 4.7.13 added it as a weekly job (Sunday 03:30); since v5.6.3 it is daily, and existing servers move to the daily schedule on cipi self-update (migration 5.6.3). A schedule changed by hand is left as it is.

After upgrading, cipi php upgrade prints one line per installed PHP version, compared with the oldest release that carries every security fix Cipi knows about. Since v5.9.1 that is 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36 — the PHP security release of 2026-11-19 — and 8.6.0, released the same day with the same fixes. Up to v5.9.0 it was 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 (the release of 2026-10-21); a server on those is reported vulnerable from v5.9.1 on: patched — at or past that release. VULNERABLE — the fix exists but this server does not have it, typically because the repository has not published it yet. Run cipi php upgrade again later. distro — a build from the Ubuntu archive, which backports fixes without changing the version number; check apt changelog php8.3-fpm . END OF LIFE — PHP 8.1 and older get no fixes from the PHP project any more. Cipi installs 8.3 and later only, so this affects servers set up before 4.5.4; move their apps with cipi app edit <app> --php=8.5 . PHP 8.2 security support ends on 2026-12-31 , and the report says so. prerelease (v5.9.1+) — a release candidate, beta or alpha: what the repository carries for a branch that is not released yet (see PHP 8.6 ). It is not compared with a security release. The release of 2026-11-19. It fixes, among others, request smuggling in PHP-FPM (CVE-2026-129289), a use-after-free in the PHP-FPM master (CVE-2026-129291), two ways to code execution through session files (CVE-2026-126714, CVE-2026-115560), a use-after-free of the timezone cache (CVE-2026-129496) and, on 8.5 and later, one in fatal-error backtraces (CVE-2026

Every PHP-FPM pool Cipi writes — app pools, Node webhook pools, and the panel API and GUI pools — turns off the two confirmed attack paths of CVE-2026-109619 (PHP security advisory of 2026-10-21, with CVE-2026-109618: unauthenticated remote code execution in every SAPI that serves web requests): php_admin_flag[session.upload_progress.enabled] = off php_admin_flag[fatal_error_backtraces] = off ; PHP 8.5 only — the setting does not exist earlier They are set as php_admin_flag , so they apply before the request is parsed and .user.ini or ini_set() cannot turn them back on. The PHP project says only the patch release is a complete fix; the flags narrow the attack until it is installed. Migration 5.6.3 renders the app and Node webhook pools again, edits the cipi-api and cipi-gui pools in place, keeps the previous pools in /var/lib/cipi/fpm-pool-backup-5.6.3/ (a version whose new pools fail php-fpm -t gets the old ones back), runs cipi php upgrade and restarts every PHP-FPM service — a restart, not a reload, because a stale worker is what CVE-2026-109619 exploits.

FrankenPHP runs the PHP built into its own binary and never reads an FPM pool. Every Octane app therefore loads the same two settings from /etc/php/cipi-octane.d/99-cipi-hardening.ini : its <app>-octane Supervisor program sets PHP_INI_SCAN_DIR=":/etc/php/cipi-octane.d" . The leading : keeps PHP's compiled-in scan directory, so the php that starts Octane still loads its conf.d , and Octane passes the variable on to FrankenPHP. session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 fatal_error_backtraces = 0 ; ignored by PHP below 8.5 The settings load at startup, so ini_set() cannot turn upload progress back on. This also covers the PHP advisory of 2026-10-23 (CVE-2026-115560, no fixed release yet), whose only mitigation is session.upload_progress.enabled=0 . Migration 5.7.1 writes the file, renders every Octane program again (previous files in /var/lib/cipi/supervisor-backup-5.7.1/ , put back if Supervisor refuses the new ones) and restarts the running ones. Optional, not a default: the advisory also suggests a lower body limit and an unlimited memory limit for servers that cannot update. Neither is applied by Cipi — a 32M body limit would break uploads that work today, and an unlimited memory limit trades this bug for runaway workers. Both are available through cipi ini set , server-wide or per app with --app=<app> : # lower body limit: upload_max_filesize first, then post_max_size cipi ini set upload_max_filesize=30M [--app=<app>] cipi ini set post_max_size=32M [--app=<app>] # unlimited memory_limit — only with a systemd MemoryMax= cap on the phpX.Y-fpm service cipi ini set memory_limit=-1

The system default is the PHP version used by the root and cipi users, the Cipi API FPM pool, and the API queue worker. Use cipi php switch <ver> to change it. The command migrates the API pool (and the GUI FPM pool when installed), recreates panel sockets, and restarts the API worker. Since 5.0.9+ , PUT /api/php/default wraps this via the panel API ( php-manage ability). Since 5.0.10–5.0.12 , switch tolerates partial update-alternatives success, remounts read-only roots when needed, and keeps API/GUI FPM pools on the target version to avoid nginx 502. REST: GET /api/php , POST /api/php/install , DELETE /api/php/{version} , PUT /api/php/default (API 1.15.0+ / Cipi 5.0.6+ ). CLI JSON: cipi php list --json (since 5.0.6 ). Each app has its own PHP version (set at app create or via cipi app edit --php= ). Deployer, Composer, crontab deploy triggers, and cipi sync import always run with the app's configured PHP — never the system default. To switch an existing app to a different version: cipi app edit myapp --php=8.5 This hot-swaps the PHP version with zero downtime: updates the FPM pool, Nginx socket, Supervisor workers, crontab, Deployer config, and .env in one atomic operation.

Available since v5.1.0 . A guided way to change PHP settings without hunting for the right php.ini . Every server-wide change reaches both SAPIs — PHP-FPM and CLI — so what your web requests see is also what queue workers, artisan and cron see. cipi ini list # effective values and which layer set them cipi ini list --app=shop # as seen by one app cipi ini get memory_limit # one setting cipi ini set upload_max_filesize=50M # server-wide (FPM + CLI) cipi ini set memory_limit=512M --app=shop # for one app only cipi ini unset memory_limit --app=shop # fall back to the wider value cipi ini reset [--app=shop] # back to Cipi defaults cipi ini keys # what can be set, and what cannot A 5.1.3 hotfix stopped cipi ini list from dying on the first setting after printing the table header ( _INI_SOURCE: unbound variable ). No migration: cipi self-update copies the new lib/ini.sh .

It raises the settings that would silently cap yours. Setting upload_max_filesize also raises post_max_size and memory_limit when they would otherwise limit it, and Nginx's client_max_body_size is flagged when it would. It refuses what should not be set this way. Settable keys are an explicit whitelist — see cipi ini keys . open_basedir , auto_prepend_file , extension and friends are refused by name, with the reason , because Cipi manages them as part of app isolation. The two keys of the 2026-10-21 PHP advisory, session.upload_progress.enabled and fatal_error_backtraces , are listed there too (5.7.2+): off in every pool since 5.6.3, in each version's fpm/conf.d/99-cipi.ini since 5.7.2. Per-app overrides win. --app=<app> writes into that app's FPM pool, which outranks the server-wide file — for that app only.

Before 5.1.0 every FPM pool hardcoded upload_max_filesize , post_max_size and max_execution_time , and pool values outrank conf.d — so a server-wide php.ini change could not reach a single app. On top of that, Cipi wrote 99-cipi.ini for FPM only, leaving the CLI SAPI (queue workers, artisan , cron) on the PHP package defaults. In 5.1.0 pools carry only what is genuinely per-app ( open_basedir , the error log, explicit overrides) and inherit everything else; both SAPIs get their file; and migration 5.1.0 backfills the CLI 99-cipi.ini and rewrites existing pools on update. Each change fires the ini_set notification trigger, so a PHP setting never changes on a shared server without a trace. An app can also carry its PHP version and per-app settings in its repository — see cipi.yml .

d: Node versions on the server and per app.
x: Available since v5.4.0 ; from the panel too ( Server → Node ) since v5.9.0 with API 1.39. Node runtimes for Node apps , and a server-wide Node for Laravel asset builds too. Official nodejs.org builds (x64 and arm64) are checked against SHASUMS256.txt , unpacked to /opt/cipi/node/v<version> and exposed as /opt/cipi/node/<major> through an atomic symlink, with corepack enabled for pnpm and yarn. Even (LTS) majors only. cipi node install 24 # official build, checksum-verified (default major: 22) cipi node list # installed majors, the default, and the apps on each cipi node upgrade 22 --restart #

h: A server-wide Node for Laravel apps
x: cipi node default <major> installs the major if needed and links node npm npx corepack pnpm pnpx yarn yarnpkg from /opt/cipi/node/<major>/bin into /usr/local/bin , which comes before NodeSource's /usr/bin on the PATH of SSH sessions (Deployer), sudo ( secure_path , cipi app run ) and each app's .bashrc . Laravel --node-build asset builds, cipi app run <app> npm … and cipi.yml deploy.post all use it from their next run. The links point at the major, not at a patch, so cipi node upgrade updates every app on the default. system removes only Cipi's links and falls back to the NodeSource package, which is never removed. A file in /usr/local/bin that Cipi did not create — a global pnpm, a hand-installed node — is left alone and named in a warning. New Node apps start on the default unless --node-version says otherwise. The default major cannot be removed. Changing it sends the node_default notification . One Laravel app can keep its own major with cipi app edit <app> --node-version=24 ; --node-version=default follows the server again. Node 20 → 22. Node 20 reached end of life in April 2026. Fresh installs get Node 22 from NodeSource. On update, migration 5.4.0 switches servers still on 20 to cipi node default 22 ; the NodeSource package stays, so cipi node default system restores 20. Servers already on another major, or with no Node, are left alone. The panel API ( 1.31+ , Cipi 5.4.1+ ) can list runtimes and read and restart Node apps ( node list|status|restart ).
